13301-the-new-ideal-in-education-an-addr:
Father Nicholai Velimirovic's New Ideal in Education, an address before the League of the Empire on July 16, 1916, reprinted from the Federal Magazine, argues that peace depends on teaching children. Velimirovic, a Serbian Orthodox priest with a doctorate, opens with nature caring for our individual sense while education must care for our panhuman sense. The address is short, urgent, and wartime.

He holds that wars will stop only when a new ideal of education is realized, summed up in one word, panhumanism, where individualism is a brick and panhumanism a building. Later, he warns that maternal love can make a child egotistic, patriotism can degenerate into chauvinism, and church schooling alone can make a bigot. The address is a plea for international education.
24131-xingu:
Edith Wharton wrote this comic novella, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1916. Mrs. Ballinger leads the Lunch Club, a band of ladies who pursue Culture together, meeting only as a group. After three or four winters of lunches and debate, the club has won local distinction, and entertaining famous strangers is now one of its accepted duties.

The next guest is the celebrated Osric Dane, invited to meet at Mrs. Bellinger's house, while Mrs. Plinth, proud of her picture gallery and her footman, thinks she should host instead. Wharton skewers polite pretension with a cool eye. Readers get a short, witty satire of culture clubs, rivalry, and the fear of being found out.
26597-how-to-behave-a-pocket-manual-of-r:
Fowler and Wells published this pocket manual of republican etiquette at New York in 1887, though it was first entered in 1857, as the third of their Hand-books for Home Improvement. Republican here means American, with manners fitted to a country without aristocratic rank. Its full subtitle promises rules for correct personal habits and the etiquette of nearly every occasion.

Chapters cover personal habits, dress, self-culture, and fundamental principles, then domestic manners and the observances of everyday life. Salutations, introductions, dinners, evening parties, letters, weddings, funerals, church, travel, and the street each get their rules. Love and courtship and rules of order for debating societies close a handbook meant to be carried and consulted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-timoleon-chem:
Timoleon Cheminais de Montaigu, a pulpit orator born at Paris in 1652, entered the Society of Jesus at fifteen and died in 1689. After teaching rhetoric and humanities at Orleans, he was set to preaching. Bayle reports that many ranked him with Bourdaloue, the great court preacher, though others thought that praise too high.

His health broke down within a few years. Named court preacher, he could not take the post as his voice partly failed, and he turned instead to teaching villagers and country folk. Bretonneau edited his sermons in four volumes at Paris in 1690 and 1691, and they were translated into German, Dutch and Italian. He also wrote Sentiments of Piety, published in 1691.
doe-osti-3002123-llms-for-mfg-on-the-sta:
William Halsey, Michael Sprayberry, and Vincent Paquit of Oak Ridge survey a fast-moving field in ORNL/TM-2025/4188, dated September 2025. Their subject is large language models, the text-trained AI systems behind modern chatbots, and what those models can do in manufacturing. The report opens with how the models work, from neural networks to fine-tuning methods such as low-rank adaptation.

Later sections map model uses onto factory work, with additive manufacturing as a main case. Topics include retrieval-augmented generation, which lets a model pull facts from stored documents, and knowledge graphs for materials data. The authors also face the known weakness of these models: confident false answers, called hallucinations. Plant engineers and researchers get a plain map of what is ready now and what is not.
doe-osti-3376044-distribution-system-pla: Distribution plans got template-guided, and this DOE slides cover electric utilities. The pages detail the system findings. The energy folks get their deck. The adaptation was by states. The deck was energy. The states were adaptation. The utilities were electric.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BringuierCarlos:
Carlos Bringuier was the Cuban exile leader in New Orleans who clashed with Lee Harvey Oswald in the summer of 1963, in a street argument and then a radio debate. He later set down his anti-Castro case in the book Red Friday, published in Chicago by Charles Hallberg and Company.

This review weighs the book, and the reviewer is unsure what to make of it. He questions whether it has real substance or is the work of 'a nut of the extreme radical right.' Reviews in researchers' files show how exile literature was received at the time. The piece preserves that judgment, harsh as it is, in its original words.
podcast-dannyjones-1o6X-ux8xgU:
Jeff Kripal teaches religious studies and has spent a career arguing that paranormal experiences deserve serious scholarly attention. With Danny Jones, the professor of ancient religion connects UFO reports and psychic phenomena to esotericism, the hidden spiritual traditions that run beneath official faiths.

Kripal's approach is comparative: he reads modern encounters beside ancient texts and mystical writings, and finds the same shapes recurring. That method sets this episode apart from the show's usual whistleblower fare. A scholar, not a believer or a debunker, leads the tour. Listeners who want the weird treated with academic care, neither worshipped nor mocked, will find Kripal's framing the most useful part of the conversation.
podcast-dannyjones-hf9Ob8mBNgU:
Matthew Cox, once the FBI's most wanted con artist, explains the art of being a snitch to Danny Jones. Cox ran a huge mortgage fraud scheme, fled, and was caught, then learned the informant game from inside prison. His confessional covers the lies that paid and the deals that followed.

Cox describes how cooperators trade information for freedom and how handlers play them. He shares tricks of persuasion he used both as a fraudster and as an informant. Jones asks where the moral lines sit in that world. Fascinated and wary listeners get a master class from a man who played both sides.
podcast-joerogan-O52aLL8ycGU:
Filmmakers Eric Goode and Jeremy McBride join Joe Rogan for episode 2536. The pair made the hit series Tiger King about big cat keepers. Their work mixes crime, ego, and wild animals.

They tell Rogan how they found that strange world and filmed it. Tales of private zoos and feuding owners fill the hour. The pair also discuss what the cameras missed. Listeners who loved the series get the backstory from the men who shot it, with new detail on a saga that never quite ends. The weirdness never lets the hour slow down.
the-new-ideal-in-education-an-address-gi:
Father Nicholai Velimirovic gave his address The New Ideal in Education before the League of the Empire. The date was July 16, 1916. A Fleet Street publisher in London reprinted it from the Federal Magazine. Its epigraph sets the theme: nature cares for our individual sense, leaving education to care for our sense of shared humanity, which Velimirovic calls the panhumanistic sense.

If we do not want war, he begins, we must look to the children; that is where the only hope lies, and the only wise starting point. Through every war, inquisition, and hour of misery, Christ has kept calling children to Him rather than kings, politicians, journalists, and generals. Velimirovic, a Serbian priest with a doctorate, asks why the grown leaders are passed over, and answers that they are too deeply engaged in a wrong state of things.
